cards.front: An {{c1::ecosystem}} is all the living things in an area and the nonliving environment they interact with, such as water, light and temperature.
cards.back: The Chesapeake Bay is one ecosystem; a single marsh inside it can be studied as another.
cards.quote: An ecosystem is all the living things in an area and the nonliving environment they interact with, such as water, light and temperature.
cards.section: Explain: who eats whom in the Bay

cards.front: A {{c1::producer}} captures energy from sunlight and stores it in food.
cards.quote: A producer captures energy from sunlight and stores it in food.
cards.section: Explain: who eats whom in the Bay

cards.front: A {{c1::consumer}} gets energy by eating other living things.
cards.quote: A consumer gets energy by eating other living things.
cards.section: Explain: who eats whom in the Bay

cards.front: A {{c1::decomposer}}, such as many bacteria and fungi, gets energy from dead matter and wastes.
cards.quote: A decomposer, such as many bacteria and fungi, gets energy from dead matter and wastes.
cards.section: Explain: who eats whom in the Bay

cards.front: A {{c1::trophic level}} is a feeding step: producers are the first level, primary consumers the second, and so on.
cards.quote: A trophic level is a feeding step: producers are the first level, primary consumers the second, and so on.
cards.section: Explain: who eats whom in the Bay

cards.front: In the open water of the Chesapeake Bay, what are the main producers?
cards.back: Phytoplankton: tiny algae and photosynthetic bacteria (cyanobacteria) that drift in the water. Underwater grasses are producers too.
cards.quote: In the open water of the Bay, the main producers are phytoplankton, tiny algae and photosynthetic bacteria (cyanobacteria) that drift in the water.
cards.section: Explain: who eats whom in the Bay

cards.front: What is the difference between a food chain and a food web?
cards.back: A food chain follows one feeding path. A food web links many food chains together, so it can show that one animal sits at more than one trophic level.
cards.quote: A food chain follows one feeding path. A food web links many food chains together.
cards.section: Explain: who eats whom in the Bay

cards.front: In a food web, which way does an arrow point, and why?
cards.back: From the food to the eater, because the arrow shows the way the energy moves. An arrow from menhaden to osprey means energy goes from menhaden into the osprey.
cards.quote: Arrows point from the food to the eater, the way the energy moves
cards.section: Explain: who eats whom in the Bay

cards.front: In a Chesapeake Bay food web, menhaden eat phytoplankton directly on one path. What consumer level is an osprey that eats that menhaden? What if zooplankton are in the path?
cards.back: Secondary on the direct path, because the menhaden is a primary consumer. With zooplankton in the path, the osprey is tertiary. An animal's level depends on the path you follow.
cards.quote: The menhaden is a primary consumer, so the osprey is secondary. With zooplankton in the path, the osprey is tertiary.
cards.section: Explain: who eats whom in the Bay

cards.front: Striped bass eat menhaden. On the path phytoplankton → zooplankton → menhaden → striped bass, what consumer level is the striped bass?
cards.back: Tertiary consumer. Zooplankton are primary, menhaden secondary, striped bass tertiary.
cards.why: Each step up the path adds one consumer level, as in the osprey path.
cards.quote: A secondary consumer eats primary consumers, and a tertiary consumer eats secondary consumers.
cards.section: Explain: who eats whom in the Bay

cards.front: When a zooplankton eats phytoplankton, where does the energy go besides new zooplankton tissue?
cards.back: Some is released as heat by cellular respiration. Parts that are not eaten, or are eaten but not digested, mostly end up with decomposers.
cards.quote: The parts that are not eaten, or eaten but not digested, mostly end up with decomposers.
cards.section: Explain: why each level gets less

cards.front: {{c1::Energy transfer efficiency}} is the percentage of the energy at one trophic level that reaches the next.
cards.back: Both levels must use the same kind of measurement.
cards.quote: Energy transfer efficiency is the percentage of the energy at one trophic level that reaches the next.
cards.section: Explain: why each level gets less

cards.front: Is 10 percent a fixed rule for energy transfer between trophic levels?
cards.back: No. It is a rough model. Real measurements are often higher or lower; a 2026 synthesis of 2,052 estimates found an average of about 6 percent, lower on land than in the sea.
cards.quote: A common rule of thumb uses about 10 percent, but real measurements are often higher or lower.
cards.section: Explain: why each level gets less

cards.front: In a model patch of Bay, phytoplankton add 50,000 kJ per square meter per year as new tissue. With 10 percent passing up at each step, how much new tissue does the menhaden level make if menhaden eat zooplankton?
cards.back: 500 kJ per square meter per year. Zooplankton: 50,000 × 0.10 = 5,000. Menhaden: 5,000 × 0.10 = 500.
cards.why: Each step multiplies by 0.10, so two steps keep one-hundredth.
cards.quote: In this model, one-thousandth of the producers' energy becomes tissue at the osprey level.
cards.section: Explain: why each level gets less

cards.front: Phytoplankton add 100,000 kJ per square meter per year as new tissue. Compare the osprey level after three steps at 5 percent transfer and at 20 percent transfer.
cards.back: 5 percent: 100,000 × 0.05 × 0.05 × 0.05 = 12.5 kJ. 20 percent: 100,000 × 0.20 × 0.20 × 0.20 = 800 kJ. The higher transfer leaves 64 times more at the top.
cards.why: The simulation lets you try 5 to 20 percent because real values spread widely.
cards.quote: Because real values spread this widely, the simulation lets you try 5 to 20 percent.
cards.section: Explain: why each level gets less

cards.front: Could a biomass pyramid be upside down while the energy pyramid for the same ecosystem stays upright?
cards.back: Yes. Biomass is measured at one moment, but energy flow is measured over time. In the English Channel, phytoplankton divide and are eaten so quickly that zooplankton can outweigh them.
cards.why: A biomass pyramid stacks mass (grams per square meter); an energy pyramid always narrows going up.
cards.quote: In the English Channel, phytoplankton divide and are eaten so quickly that zooplankton can outweigh them.
cards.section: Explain: why each level gets less

cards.front: Why do food chains rarely have more than about five levels?
cards.back: The shrinking energy supply is one likely reason: only part of the energy becomes tissue at each step, so little is left for the top levels.
cards.quote: The shrinking supply is one likely reason food chains rarely have more than about five levels.
cards.section: Explain: why each level gets less

cards.front: How does energy move through an ecosystem such as the Bay?
cards.back: One way: in from the source (sunlight in the Bay) and out as heat. It does not cycle back to producers.
cards.quote: Much of the carbon can cycle back to plankton, but the energy cannot.
cards.section: Evaluate: check your thinking

cards.front: Compare energy and matter such as carbon in an ecosystem: what happens to each as it moves between levels?
cards.back: Much energy is released as heat and flows one way. Carbon atoms are passed on or released, not destroyed, and mostly cycle and are used again.
cards.quote: Key idea: energy flows through ecosystems and leaves as heat, while matter cycles and can be reused.
cards.section: Explain: energy flows, matter cycles

cards.front: A deep-sea vent community has no sunlight. Does energy still flow one way through it?
cards.back: Yes. The source is chemical energy instead of sunlight, but energy still comes in from that source and leaves as heat, while matter cycles.
cards.quote: a few ecosystems, such as deep-sea vent communities, run on chemical energy instead of sunlight
cards.section: Explain: energy flows, matter cycles

cards.front: Lindeman's Cedar Bog Lake totals measured energy taken in by each level. Why are they larger than the new tissue each level built?
cards.back: They include energy each level later released as heat in respiration, which is not part of new tissue.
cards.quote: They include energy each level later released as heat in respiration, so they are larger than the new tissue each level built.
cards.section: Elaborate: real energy budgets and osprey diets

cards.front: In Cedar Bog Lake, primary consumers took in 14.8 and secondary consumers 3.1 gram-calories per square centimeter per year. What percent passed from primary to secondary consumers?
cards.back: About 20.9 percent. 3.1 ÷ 14.8 × 100 = 20.9. Divide each level by the one below it.
cards.quote: Primary to secondary consumers is 3.1 ÷ 14.8 × 100, about 20.9 percent.
cards.section: Elaborate: real energy budgets and osprey diets

cards.front: At lower-estuary osprey nests, menhaden were 24.2 percent of fish counted but 44.7 percent of prey energy. Why might the two shares differ, and what can the table not show?
cards.back: Fish differ in size and energy content, so a smaller share by count can supply more energy. The table cannot show which difference caused the pattern.
cards.quote: Fish differ in size and energy content. A smaller share by count can supply more energy.
cards.section: Elaborate: real energy budgets and osprey diets

cards.front: Mobjack Bay osprey nests had a menhaden share of diet of 67.3 percent in 1985, 24.7 percent in 2006–2007 and 30.2 percent in 2021. Upper-estuary nests in 2006–2007 had 1.5 percent by count. What broad claim about ospreys and menhaden do these data support?
cards.back: Only that the menhaden link varies from place to place and year to year. Each number describes a place, a year or both, so one sample cannot support a broad conclusion.
cards.quote: Ospreys show that the menhaden link varies from place to place and year to year.
cards.section: Elaborate: real energy budgets and osprey diets

cards.front: You test whether extra menhaden at osprey nests raises the share of nests that raise young. What is the control group, and why does it need the same visits?
cards.back: Nests that get no extra fish but are visited the same way. The visits are held constant so the only difference between groups is the extra food.
cards.quote: Control: nests that get no extra fish but are visited the same way.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In the osprey feeding study, some nests can only be control because boats cannot reach them. What should you do about this, and why?
cards.back: Say so, because it could bias the result. Random assignment of nests to groups is the aim, so a limit on it must be reported.
cards.quote: If some nests can only be control, as when boats cannot reach them, say so, because it could bias the result.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In a Mobjack Bay experiment, 13 of 16 osprey nests given extra menhaden raised young, compared with 5 of 15 control nests. What does this support, and what does it not say?
cards.back: About 81 percent of fed nests and 33 percent of control nests raised young, so it supports food limitation at that site. It does not say why fish are scarce.
cards.quote: What results mean: higher success in the fed group supports food limitation at that site. It does not say why fish are scarce.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: An osprey chick's energy began as sunlight. A student says decomposers return the chick's energy to phytoplankton, as they do its carbon. How do you reply?
cards.back: Carbon can cycle back to plankton, but energy cannot. At each feeding step the rest spreads as heat or stays in matter for decomposers, so energy leaves as heat.
cards.why: Matter cycles; energy flows one way.
cards.quote: Much of the carbon can cycle back to plankton, but the energy cannot.
cards.section: Evaluate: check your thinking
